title: Immune Responses in Pulmonary Disease
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: The lung exchanges gas across about 70 square meters of alveolar surface while breathing in about 10,000 L of air a day, so it must clear microbes and particles without inflaming the alveoli. This chapter explains the layered innate defenses, then shows how each hypersensitivity type produces a distinct lung disease: IgE in asthma, antibody to basement membrane in Goodpasture syndrome, immune complexes and T cells in hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and Th1 granulomas in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis. It closes with how respiratory vaccines work and how lung cancers escape immunity. Board questions usually give a clinical picture and ask for the hypersensitivity type, cytokine, antibody target, or defense that failed.
prerequisites: Innate and adaptive immunity, antigen presentation on MHC class I and II (IM units)
The four Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity types
Airway and alveolar histology: ciliated epithelium, goblet cells, type I and II pneumocytes
Obstructive versus restrictive patterns on pulmonary function tests
B cell class switching and the germinal center reaction

connections.how: Every disease here is a standard hypersensitivity or immune evasion mechanism expressed in lung tissue.
Loss of a specific defense predicts which organisms cause pneumonia, such as encapsulated bacteria when opsonizing antibody is lacking.
Asthma is the prototype of reversible obstruction, while hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis produce restriction and a low DLCO.
Goodpasture syndrome and granulomatosis with polyangiitis are pulmonary renal syndromes with crescentic glomerulonephritis.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome is explained by reduced presynaptic Ca2+ entry and acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction.

Dimeric IgA joined by a J chain and carried across epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, a fragment of which remains as secretory component.
Soluble C-type lectins, including surfactant proteins A and D, that bind microbial carbohydrates and promote their clearance.
A molecule that coats a particle and makes it easier for phagocytes to bind and ingest.
A CD4 helper T cell subset that secretes IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and drives IgE, eosinophil, and mucus responses.
The second wave of a type I response, several hours after exposure, caused by recruited eosinophils, Th2 cells, and other leukocytes.
An organized collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleated giant cells, surrounded by lymphocytes.
An IFN-gamma activated macrophage with abundant pink cytoplasm and an elongated nucleus that resembles an epithelial cell.

A vaccine in which a bacterial capsular polysaccharide is covalently linked to a carrier protein so that helper T cells can assist the antibody response.

sections.title: Innate lung defenses and how their failure causes pneumonia

blocks.text: The lower respiratory tract below the larynx is kept nearly sterile by defenses arranged in layers. Which layer handles an inhaled particle depends mainly on its size, because size determines where it deposits: by impaction in the nose and large airways, by sedimentation in small airways, and by diffusion in the alveoli.

blocks.title: Layers of lung defense
rows: Turbulent flow makes particles larger than about 10 micrometers impact on the mucosa
Vagal afferents trigger forceful expiration that expels material; the epiglottis and glottis close during swallowing
Particles of about 2 to 10 micrometers stick to mucus that cilia carry up to the pharynx to be swallowed or coughed out
IgA blocks microbial attachment without inflammation; the others kill or starve bacteria
Ingest particles of about 0.5 to 5 micrometers and microbes; recruit neutrophils if the load is large
Bind microbial surface carbohydrates, aggregate organisms, and opsonize them for macrophages
blocks.caption: Size cutoffs are approximate and overlap; smaller particles travel deeper.

blocks.text: The mucociliary escalator has two parts. Goblet cells and submucosal glands make a gel layer of mucus, which floats on a thin watery periciliary layer. Ciliated cells, each with a few hundred cilia built on a 9 + 2 microtubule axoneme, beat in coordinated waves; dynein arms between the outer microtubule doublets use ATP to slide them and bend the cilium. The beat moves the gel layer toward the pharynx, so a defect in mucus hydration, in cilia, or in cough leaves material to stagnate.

Secretory IgA is made by plasma cells in the lamina propria as a dimer joined by a J chain. The polymeric immunoglobulin receptor on the basal surface of the epithelium carries it across, and part of the receptor stays bound as secretory component, which protects IgA from proteases. IgA neutralizes toxins and blocks adhesion but activates complement poorly, so it protects without inflaming the mucosa. Surfactant proteins A and D are hydrophilic collectins secreted by type II pneumocytes and club cells. Unlike SP-B and SP-C, which lower surface tension, SP-A and SP-D bind sugars on bacteria, viruses, and fungi and present them to macrophages.
Why smoking, alcohol, and ciliary defects raise pneumonia risk

Cigarette smoke slows ciliary beating, causes goblet cell hyperplasia with thicker mucus, replaces ciliated cells with squamous metaplasia, and impairs the killing ability of alveolar macrophages, so organisms that should be carried out are retained. Alcohol depresses consciousness, cough, and the gag reflex, which allows aspiration of oropharyngeal flora, including anaerobes and Klebsiella pneumoniae, and it also impairs neutrophil and macrophage function. In primary ciliary dyskinesia, an autosomal recessive defect most often in dynein arm proteins, cilia are immotile or beat abnormally, causing chronic sinusitis, otitis media, and bronchiectasis from childhood. About half of patients have situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome) because embryonic nodal cilia set left and right asymmetry, and men are usually infertile because sperm flagella share the axoneme. Cystic fibrosis is a different mechanism: the cilia are normal, but dehydrated mucus cannot be moved.

blocks.predict: A patient with immotile cilia and a patient with cystic fibrosis both develop bronchiectasis. Would situs inversus or a nasal biopsy with abnormal cilia help separate them?
blocks.explain: Yes. Primary ciliary dyskinesia is a structural ciliary defect, so electron microscopy shows missing dynein arms and half of patients have situs inversus. In cystic fibrosis the CFTR defect dehydrates the periciliary layer; cilia are structurally normal and organ position is normal.
blocks.check: The mucociliary escalator paragraph and the final paragraph on ciliary defects.

sections.title: Type I hypersensitivity in allergic asthma and rhinitis

blocks.text: Allergic asthma and allergic rhinitis are type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions: IgE bound to mast cells reacts with an inhaled allergen such as house dust mite, pollen, animal dander, or cockroach protein. The same mechanism affects the nasal mucosa in rhinitis and the bronchi in asthma, and the two often occur together in atopic people, who have an inherited tendency to make IgE responses.

blocks.title: Sensitization and the allergic asthma attack
steps: Dendritic cells carry inhaled allergen to lymph nodes
Epithelial alarmins and IL-4 push naive CD4 cells to Th2
Th2 IL-4 and CD40 ligand switch B cells to IgE
IgE binds Fc epsilon RI on mast cells (sensitized)
Re-exposure cross-links bound IgE; mast cells degranulate
Minutes: bronchoconstriction, mucus, edema (early phase)
Hours: IL-5 recruited eosinophils and Th2 cells (late phase)
blocks.caption: The first exposure sensitizes without symptoms; later exposures trigger the reaction.

blocks.text: Sensitization begins when the injured or stimulated airway epithelium releases alarmins (IL-25, IL-33, and thymic stromal lymphopoietin), which favor Th2 differentiation. Th2 cytokines then each produce one feature of the disease. IL-4, with CD40 ligand on the T cell, drives B cell class switching to IgE. IL-5 drives eosinophil production in the marrow, their activation, and their survival. IL-13 acts on airway epithelium and smooth muscle to cause goblet cell metaplasia, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyperresponsiveness, and it also supports IgE switching. IgE binds the high-affinity receptor Fc epsilon RI on mast cells and basophils, where it remains for weeks.

When allergen cross-links two or more receptor-bound IgE molecules, the mast cell degranulates within minutes. Preformed mediators (histamine, tryptase, heparin) are released at once, and arachidonic acid is converted to newly synthesized mediators: the cysteinyl leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 and prostaglandin D2, which are potent bronchoconstrictors and increase vascular permeability and mucus secretion. Mast cells also release cytokines and chemokines that set up the late phase.

blocks.title: Early and late phase responses
rows: Within minutes; fades in about 1 hour
About 4 to 8 hours; may last a day or more
Recruited eosinophils, Th2 cells, basophils, neutrophils
Histamine, leukotrienes C4, D4, E4, prostaglandin D2
Major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein, leukotrienes, Th2 cytokines
Epithelial damage, persistent inflammation, increased hyperresponsiveness
blocks.caption: Repeated late phase reactions lead to chronic airway remodeling.

blocks.text: Eosinophil granule proteins injure the epithelium, exposing sensory nerves and removing epithelial barrier function, which explains why hyperresponsiveness rises after the late phase. Repeated cycles remodel the airway: a thickened subepithelial basement membrane from collagen deposition, smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, goblet cell and submucosal gland hyperplasia, and mucus plugs. Sputum may show Curschmann spirals (shed epithelium in mucus casts of small airways) and Charcot-Leyden crystals (crystallized eosinophil protein). Narrowed airways produce wheeze and an obstructive pattern with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio that improves substantially after a bronchodilator, and blood eosinophils and total IgE are often raised. In rhinitis, histamine stimulates sensory nerves (itch, sneezing) and dilates leaky vessels (rhinorrhea, congestion), and the mucosa looks pale and swollen.

sections.title: Granulomas in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis and the role of TNF-alpha

blocks.text: A granuloma is a type IV (delayed, cell-mediated) response that walls off an antigen macrophages cannot destroy. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the classic example: inhaled bacilli are ingested by alveolar macrophages, but cell wall lipids such as sulfatides and lipoarabinomannan, together with bacterial proteins, block fusion of the phagosome with the lysosome, so the organism survives and multiplies inside the cell.

blocks.title: How a granuloma forms and is maintained
steps: Macrophage ingests an organism it cannot kill
Macrophage presents antigen on MHC class II and secretes IL-12
IL-12 drives naive CD4 cells to become Th1 cells
Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma
IFN-gamma activates macrophages: phagolysosome fusion, nitric oxide
Activated macrophages become epithelioid and giant cells
TNF-alpha recruits cells and holds the granuloma together
blocks.caption: The same Th1 pathway is used in tuberculosis and in sarcoidosis; only the antigen differs.

blocks.text: IFN-gamma is the key activating signal. It enables phagolysosome fusion, induces inducible nitric oxide synthase, and increases antigen presentation, turning macrophages into epithelioid cells that may fuse into multinucleated giant cells (Langhans giant cells, not Langerhans cells, with nuclei in a horseshoe). A cuff of CD4 T cells surrounds them. TNF-alpha, made mainly by macrophages and T cells, induces chemokines and endothelial adhesion molecules that keep recruiting cells, and it acts with IFN-gamma to keep macrophages activated. In tuberculosis the intense response to mycobacterial lipids produces caseous necrosis, a cheesy center of dead cells, and the granuloma contains rather than eliminates the organism; this contained state is latent infection. The tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assay detect this Th1 memory, not active disease. People with inherited defects in the IL-12 or IFN-gamma receptors develop disseminated mycobacterial infection, which confirms the pathway.

blocks.title: Tuberculosis and sarcoidosis granulomas
rows: Unknown; exaggerated Th1 response to a persistent antigen
Ghon complex in primary; apical cavities in reactivation
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, with or without interstitial disease
Positive culture or nucleic acid test
Raised serum ACE; hypercalcemia; high CD4 to CD8 ratio in lavage fluid
blocks.caption: Neither inclusion nor ACE is diagnostic; sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion.

blocks.text: Sarcoidosis granulomas are formed by the same Th1 mechanism, driven by CD4 T cells concentrated in the lung while peripheral skin test responses are often reduced (cutaneous anergy). Activated granuloma macrophages produce angiotensin converting enzyme and express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol without normal feedback control, which explains hypercalciuria and hypercalcemia.

blocks.title: Predicting tuberculosis reactivation under TNF-alpha blockade
blocks.text: A patient with a positive interferon-gamma release assay and a normal chest radiograph has latent tuberculosis: live bacilli are contained inside granulomas. A monoclonal antibody that neutralizes TNF-alpha is started for an autoimmune disease. Without TNF-alpha, chemokine and adhesion molecule signals that recruit and retain cells fall, macrophage activation weakens, and the granuloma loses its organized structure. Bacilli are released and multiply, usually within the first months. Because containment fails everywhere at once, the resulting disease is often extrapulmonary or disseminated rather than typical apical cavitation. The same reasoning explains why granulomatous fungal infections such as histoplasmosis can also reactivate.

sections.title: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis and how it differs from asthma

blocks.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis) is an immune reaction in the alveolar walls and terminal bronchioles to an inhaled organic antigen. Farmer lung is the prototype: thermophilic actinomycetes, such as Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula, grow in warm, moldy hay and release spores small enough (under about 5 micrometers) to reach the alveoli. Bird fancier lung (avian proteins in droppings and feathers) and hot tub lung (nontuberculous mycobacteria in aerosols) work the same way. Asthma antigens, by contrast, act mainly in the conducting airways.

Two hypersensitivity types combine. Repeated exposure induces precipitating IgG. When a large dose of antigen is inhaled again, antigen and IgG form immune complexes in the alveolar walls (type III), activate complement, and attract neutrophils. Complex formation and neutrophil recruitment take hours, which is why fever, chills, cough, and dyspnea begin about 4 to 8 hours after exposure and settle within a day or two once exposure stops. With continued exposure the response shifts to T cells (type IV): lymphocytes, many of them CD8 cells, infiltrate the interstitium around bronchioles, and macrophages form small, loose, poorly formed noncaseating granulomas. Over months to years this can progress to interstitial fibrosis.

Because the inflammation thickens and later scars the alveolar walls, the lung becomes stiff and gas transfer falls. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern (reduced total lung capacity and FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio) and a reduced DLCO, and lavage fluid shows a marked lymphocytosis. Serum precipitins prove exposure but not disease, because many exposed people who stay well also have them.

blocks.title: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis versus allergic asthma
rows: Organic dust: actinomycetes, avian proteins, fungi
Minutes, with a late phase at 4 to 8 hours
Mucus plugs, eosinophils, thick basement membrane
Obstructive, reversible, normal or high DLCO
blocks.caption: The late phase of asthma also starts hours after exposure, so timing alone does not separate them; site, cell type, fever, and the PFT pattern do.

blocks.predict: A dairy farmer has fever, dyspnea, and crackles every evening after forking hay in winter. Would you expect wheeze, eosinophilia, and a low FEV1/FVC ratio?
blocks.explain: No. This is hypersensitivity pneumonitis. The reaction is immune complex and T cell inflammation in the alveolar walls, not IgE in the bronchi, so it causes crackles, fever, neutrophils then lymphocytes, and a restrictive pattern with low DLCO.

sections.title: Goodpasture syndrome versus granulomatosis with polyangiitis

blocks.text: Both diseases cause a pulmonary renal syndrome, bleeding into the alveoli together with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, but by different immune mechanisms. Recognizing the mechanism explains the immunofluorescence pattern, the upper airway findings, and the serology.

Goodpasture syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane disease) is type II hypersensitivity: IgG binds a fixed tissue antigen, the noncollagenous (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. This chain is found in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, which is why these two organs are hit. The antibody binds evenly along the basement membrane, giving smooth linear IgG and C3 staining on immunofluorescence. Complement activation and Fc receptor engagement recruit neutrophils and monocytes, which break the capillary walls, so blood enters the alveoli and Bowman space and crescents form. Glomerular endothelium is fenestrated, giving circulating antibody direct access to the basement membrane, whereas alveolar capillary endothelium is continuous, so lung hemorrhage is more likely when the alveolar membrane is already injured, especially by smoking or inhaled hydrocarbons. HLA-DR15 increases susceptibility. Patients present with hemoptysis, iron deficiency anemia, hematuria with red cell casts, and rising creatinine; lavage fluid shows hemosiderin-laden macrophages.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis) is a necrotizing vasculitis of small and medium vessels with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower respiratory tract. Most patients have antibodies to proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA), which give a cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) pattern. Cytokines such as TNF-alpha, released during infection, prime neutrophils so that PR3 moves to the cell surface. ANCA then bind it and engage Fc receptors, causing neutrophils to adhere to endothelium, degranulate, release reactive oxygen species, and form extracellular traps that destroy the vessel wall. Because injury is caused by activated neutrophils rather than deposited antibody, the kidney shows few or no immune deposits (pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis).

blocks.title: Two pulmonary renal syndromes
rows: Type II: IgG to alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
Sinusitis, otitis, nasal ulcers, saddle nose
Nodules that cavitate; may also bleed
blocks.caption: Microscopic polyangiitis resembles granulomatosis with polyangiitis but has MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) and no granulomas.

blocks.text: The upper airway is the most useful distinction: chronic sinusitis, crusting nasal ulcers, and collapse of the nasal cartilage (saddle nose) point to granulomatosis with polyangiitis. About a third of patients with anti-GBM antibody also have ANCA (double positive).

sections.title: How toxoid, acellular pertussis, and conjugate vaccines protect

blocks.text: A vaccine protects only if it induces the effector that blocks the organism's main weapon. Diphtheria and tetanus cause disease mainly through exotoxins, Hib and pneumococcus through polysaccharide capsules that resist phagocytosis, and pertussis through adhesins plus toxins, so each needs a different antigen.

A toxoid is a toxin inactivated chemically, usually with formaldehyde, so it loses toxicity but keeps its epitopes. Diphtheria toxin and tetanospasmin are A-B toxins: the B subunit binds a host receptor and the A subunit acts inside the cell (diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 and stops protein synthesis; tetanospasmin cleaves synaptobrevin in inhibitory interneurons). Because toxoids are proteins, they are T cell dependent antigens, and helper T cells drive class switching to high-affinity neutralizing IgG and memory. Antitoxin IgG blocks binding of the toxin to its receptor. The immunity is antitoxic, not antibacterial, so a vaccinated person can still carry Corynebacterium diphtheriae while being protected from toxin-mediated disease.

Acellular pertussis vaccine contains purified Bordetella pertussis proteins instead of killed whole bacteria: pertussis toxoid with, depending on the product, filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbrial antigens. Antibody to the toxoid neutralizes pertussis toxin, while antibodies to the adhesins hinder attachment to ciliated respiratory epithelium. Antibody levels and protection after acellular vaccination wane over several years.

Capsular polysaccharides behave differently. Their long chains of repeating sugar units cross-link many B cell receptors at once and activate B cells without T cell help (T cell independent antigens). Because carbohydrates cannot be processed into peptides for MHC class II, helper T cells are never engaged, so the response is mostly IgM with little class switching, affinity maturation, or memory, and a repeat dose gives no booster rise. Children under about 2 years respond poorly because their marginal zone B cells, which carry most of these responses, are immature. This is why infants are especially susceptible to encapsulated bacteria.

blocks.title: Linked recognition in a conjugate vaccine
steps: Polysaccharide-specific B cell binds the conjugate by its receptor
B cell internalizes and processes the carrier protein
Carrier peptides are displayed on MHC class II
Carrier-specific helper T cell recognizes the peptide
CD40 ligand and cytokines drive germinal center reaction
IgG to the polysaccharide, affinity maturation, memory B cells
blocks.caption: The antibody is against the polysaccharide even though the T cell recognizes the protein.

blocks.title: Plain polysaccharide versus conjugate vaccine
rows: Reduced, which also protects unvaccinated contacts
Hib (PRP capsule linked to tetanus toxoid or other carrier), pneumococcal conjugate
blocks.caption: Conjugation converts a T cell independent antigen into a T cell dependent one.

blocks.title: Why the conjugate antibody targets the sugar
blocks.text: The Hib capsule is polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP). In the conjugate vaccine PRP is linked to a carrier such as tetanus toxoid. A B cell whose receptor recognizes PRP binds the conjugate and swallows the whole molecule. It cannot present PRP to T cells, but it does present tetanus toxoid peptides on MHC class II. A helper T cell that recognizes those peptides delivers CD40 ligand and cytokines to that B cell, and the B cell, still specific for PRP, class switches and enters a germinal center. The resulting memory B cells and plasma cells make IgG against PRP, which opsonizes the bacterium and activates complement. Help from the carrier is the only change; the specificity comes from the B cell receptor.

sections.title: Immune evasion by lung cancer and paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes

blocks.text: Lung cancers, especially those caused by smoking, carry many mutations, so they make many abnormal proteins (neoantigens). Tumor cells process these into peptides presented on MHC class I, where CD8 cytotoxic T cells can recognize and kill them. A tumor that grows to clinical size has therefore usually acquired ways to avoid this response.

blocks.title: How lung cancers escape T cells
rows: Loss or mutation of HLA genes or beta-2 microglobulin, or reduced antigen processing (for example TAP)
CD8 T cells cannot see tumor peptides
PD-L1 on tumor cells binds PD-1 on activated T cells; PD-1 recruits a phosphatase that dampens T cell receptor and CD28 signaling
T cells in the tumor are present but exhausted
Regulatory T cells, TGF-beta, IL-10, myeloid suppressor cells
Local T cell activation is blunted
blocks.caption: Tumors often use several mechanisms at once.

blocks.text: Loss of MHC class I should make tumor cells targets for natural killer cells, whose inhibitory receptors recognize class I (missing self), so tumors that escape this way must also evade NK cells, for example by shedding activating NK ligands. PD-L1 expression is often induced by IFN-gamma released from the T cells attacking the tumor, a self-protective response called adaptive resistance. Antibodies that block PD-1 or PD-L1 remove this brake, which is the mechanistic proof that the pathway restrains antitumor T cells; the same release explains why such antibodies can cause autoimmune inflammation.
Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes

Small cell lung carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor that expresses proteins normally restricted to neurons. An immune response against the tumor therefore also attacks the nervous system, and the neurologic syndrome often appears before the cancer is found. Anti-Hu antibodies target HuD, an RNA-binding protein inside neuronal nuclei; because the antigen is intracellular, the antibody is mainly a marker, and cytotoxic T cells cause the neuronal loss. The results are paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis, limbic encephalitis, and sensory neuronopathy from destruction of dorsal root ganglion cells. Antibodies to P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels are directly pathogenic: they reduce the number of presynaptic channels, so less Ca2+ enters the nerve terminal and fewer acetylcholine quanta are released, producing Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

blocks.title: Why Lambert-Eaton weakness improves with effort
blocks.text: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome each action potential lets too little Ca2+ into the nerve terminal, so acetylcholine release, and the end plate potential, falls below threshold at many fibers. Reflexes are reduced and proximal limbs are weak. If the patient contracts a muscle hard for about 10 seconds, impulses arrive faster than Ca2+ can be cleared, so residual Ca2+ accumulates and each later impulse releases more transmitter. Strength and reflexes briefly improve, and high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation shows an increment in the muscle action potential. Myasthenia gravis is the opposite: postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors are lost, release is normal, and weakness worsens with repeated use. Reduced acetylcholine release at autonomic synapses also explains the dry mouth and orthostatic symptoms of Lambert-Eaton.

integration.text: The lung shows every hypersensitivity type because it is constantly exposed to foreign material and has a thin, richly vascular basement membrane. Antigen size and site decide the disease: proteins deposited in conducting airways of atopic people give IgE responses (type I), organic dusts reaching alveoli give immune complex and T cell injury (types III and IV), persistent intracellular organisms give Th1 granulomas (type IV), and an autoantigen shared by alveolar and glomerular basement membranes gives antibody-mediated injury (type II). Histology confirms the mechanism: eosinophils and mucus plugs, loose interstitial granulomas, organized caseating or noncaseating granulomas, linear IgG, or pauci-immune necrosis.

The same immunology explains protection and its limits. Innate barriers fail mechanically (cilia, cough, mucus) before adaptive immunity is needed; vaccines work only if they engage T cell help when lasting IgG is required; and cancer exploits the checkpoints that normally prevent autoimmunity, while cross-reaction between tumor and neuron shows how an antitumor response can itself cause disease. Hypersensitivity labels are simplifications: most real diseases, including asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, involve more than one mechanism.

summary: Particle size sets where defenses act: the nose traps large particles, the mucociliary escalator clears mid-sized ones, and alveolar macrophages aided by SP-A and SP-D opsonins clear the smallest.
Smoking (ciliary and macrophage damage), alcohol (aspiration, weak cough and phagocytes), and dynein arm defects (primary ciliary dyskinesia) each remove a defense layer and raise pneumonia risk.
Allergic asthma is type I: IL-4 switches B cells to IgE, IL-5 drives eosinophils, IL-13 drives mucus and hyperresponsiveness; mast cell mediators cause the early phase and eosinophils the late phase.
Granulomas form when macrophage IL-12 drives Th1 cells whose IFN-gamma activates macrophages; TNF-alpha maintains the granuloma, so blocking it can reactivate latent tuberculosis.
Tuberculosis granulomas caseate; sarcoidosis granulomas do not and are linked to hilar adenopathy, raised ACE, and calcitriol-driven hypercalcemia.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a type III and IV reaction to organic dust in the alveolar walls, with fever hours after exposure, lymphocytes, poorly formed granulomas, and a restrictive pattern with low DLCO.

Goodpasture syndrome is type II anti-alpha-3 type IV collagen IgG with linear staining, alveolar hemorrhage, and crescentic glomerulonephritis; granulomatosis with polyangiitis is PR3-ANCA vasculitis with upper airway disease and pauci-immune glomerulonephritis.
Toxoids induce neutralizing antitoxin IgG; plain polysaccharides give T cell independent IgM without memory; conjugates add carrier-driven T cell help, giving IgG and memory even in infants.
Lung cancers evade CD8 T cells by lowering MHC class I and expressing PD-L1; small cell carcinoma shares neuronal antigens, causing anti-Hu syndromes and anti-calcium channel Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
